newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn cabinet sets change to Bundesbank law for EMU.
newsitem.headline: Bonn cabinet sets change to Bundesbank law for EMU.

text.p: The German cabinet on Tuesday approved a new draft to the law governing its central bank, the Bundesbank, which adjusts its statutes readying it for monetary union from 1999.

The law, parts of which will only take effect once Germany enters the single currency, transfers power for monetary policy to the European central bank and makes changes to bring German monetary authorities into line with others in the EU.
Under the terms of the new law, the independence of the already fiercely-autonomous central bank from the Bonn government will be strengthened even further.

A provision allowing the members of the federal cabinet who may attend Bundesbank council meetings as non-voting members to request that a decision be deferred for up to two weeks will be deleted in the new version.
And the minimum period for which a Bundesbank council member may be appointed is extended to five years from two.
The longer time period is seen as increasing continuity, but also as reducing the chances for "political" appointees.

German Finance Minister Theo Waigel, who presented the draft to the cabinet today, said the changes were necessary to anchor the central bank in its future role as part of the European System of Central Banks (ESCB).

Under a single currency, the ESCB, which will comprise the national central banks of countries within EMU, will help the European Central Bank implement its policy as well as carrying out regular non-policy central bank functions in their home country.

Under a special clause in the new law, the Bundesbank will remain responsible for issuing mark notes and coins even once the single currency has been launched, during the transition period when no euro-denominated cash will be issued.
This right will be ceded once euro notes and coins enter circulation in 2002.
